reason: The sources provide enough factual material for a surprising 45-second story with at least 10 sourced claims.
story: On January 22, 1879, British commander Lord Chelmsford rode out of his base at Isandlwana, certain the Zulu army was far away. He left over 1,300 men camped in the open without digging trenches or forming defensive wagon circles. What Chelmsford did not know was that 20,000 Zulu warriors had outmanoeuvred him, hiding silently just over a nearby ridge. When an accidental British patrol stumbled onto them, the Zulu army rose as one, deploying their legendary horns and chest of the buffalo formation. As a partial solar eclipse plunged the battlefield into an eerie twilight, the Zulus overwhelmed the British lines and wiped out the camp in less than two hours. It remains one of the worst defeats in the history of the British Empire.
angle: A total of 20,000 Zulu warriors sat in total silence, hidden just over a ridge from an unfortified British camp, until an accidental patrol walked right into them.

claims.claim: The Battle of Isandlwana took place on 22 January 1879.
Lord Chelmsford left approximately 1,300 men to guard the camp at Isandlwana.
The main Zulu force consisted of approximately 20,000 warriors.
The British camp at Isandlwana was established without entrenchments or a defensive laager.
A British scouting patrol accidentally discovered the hidden Zulu army in the morning of 22 January.
The Zulus attacked using their traditional 'horns and chest of the buffalo' formation.
Over 1,300 British and colonial troops were killed during the battle.
A solar eclipse occurred on the day of the battle, darkening the sky during the engagement.
Sir Bartle Frere presented an unacceptable ultimatum to Zulu King Cetshwayo in December 1878.
The Zulus captured about 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles, two field guns, and large amounts of ammunition and supplies.
Simultaneously on the same day, a Zulu force attacked the garrison at Rorke's Drift.
The war eventually ended after the British victory at the Battle of Ulundi on July 4, 1879.

disputed: Whether ammunition box lids were screwed shut with rusted screws causing a fatal shortage of ammunition, or whether most men in the firing line did not actually run out of ammunition. Scripts should attribute this to one account or mention it as a debated factor.
